items.title: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024
items.locator: Section 4, Principle O (PDF p.13); Provisions 28 and 29 (PDF p.14)
items.quote: determine the nature and extent of the principal risks the company is willing to take in order to achieve its long-term strategic objectives
items.why: The board-level duty behind the question. Applies to companies with a listing in the commercial companies or closed-ended investment funds category, on a comply or explain basis. Does not mention AI and does not use the words 'risk appetite'. Provision 28 asks for a robust assessment of emerging and principal risks; Provision 29 for an annual review of material controls.

items.title: Corporate Governance Code Guidance
items.quote: The board, supported by its committees and based on the recommendations from the management, should approve the company’s risk appetite
items.why: Says what a board does with appetite: approve it, check it fits the company's tolerance, see it defined, embedded in decision-making, reviewed and communicated. Paragraph 272 lists new technologies, with artificial intelligence as the example, among risks whose controls may be material. Not mandatory. Page shows 'Last updated: 3 June 2026'.

items.title: The Orange Book: Management of Risk - Principles and Concepts
items.locator: Section A, paragraph A3; Section D, paragraphs D6, D14 and D15
items.quote: The board should determine and continuously assess the nature and extent of the principal risks
items.why: Public sector equivalent: the board determines its risk appetite, decisions are compared with it, and reports show whether each principal risk is within it. The PDF edition carries Crown copyright 2023; the HTML page read here shows 'Updated 29 July 2026'. The separate Risk Appetite Guidance Note was deleted from the collection page on 29 July 2026 as out of date, so it is not cited.

items.title: SS1/23 Model risk management principles for banks
items.publisher: Bank of England, Prudential Regulation Authority
items.locator: Principle 2.1 'Board of directors’ responsibilities', points (c) and (d), PDF p.14
items.quote: The board should set a model risk appetite that articulates the level and types of model risk the firm is willing to accept.
items.why: A regulator spelling out what an appetite for model risk contains: limits on model use, thresholds for acceptable performance and tolerance for errors, and regular reports to the board against it. Banks with internal model approval only; in effect from 17 May 2024.

items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: What are the accountability and governance implications of AI?
items.locator: Section 'How should we set a meaningful risk appetite?'
items.quote: It is unrealistic to adopt a ‘zero tolerance’ approach to risks to rights and freedoms
items.why: Source of the quotation (the sentence continues 'and indeed the law does not require you to do so'). The same section says 'In all cases, you need to ensure you comply with data protection requirements', so appetite operates above the legal floor. Later it asks that decisions on trade-offs be shown to fit 'your overall risk appetite'. Marked under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. No date printed; page metadata gives 11 December 2024.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Section 1.2.2 'Risk Tolerance', p.7; GOVERN 1.3, Table 1, p.22; MAP 1.5, Table 2, p.26
items.quote: Where established guidelines do not exist, organizations should define reasonable risk tolerance.
items.why: International comparator. The framework does not prescribe a tolerance; it asks that organisational risk tolerances are determined and documented, and notes they change over time. Voluntary, United States.

items.title: International AI Safety Report 2026
items.publisher: International AI Safety Report (chair: Yoshua Bengio)
items.locator: Section 3.2 'Risk management practices', entries 'Risk thresholds/risk tiers' and 'Risk tolerance'
items.quote: Risk tolerance refers to the level of risk that an organisation is willing to accept.
items.why: Independent evidence that AI risk tolerances are 'often set implicitly through company policies and practices'. About developers of general-purpose AI, not boards of deploying organisations.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 99: Penalties
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000
items.why: Source of the figure: breach of the Article 5 prohibitions carries fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or, for an undertaking, up to 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. For SMEs the lower of the two applies (Art. 99(6)). The page prints the numbers with spaces. Commission's copy of the consolidated text, stated on the page to be based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026, with Digital Omnibus changes marked NEW or AMENDED.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 5: Prohibited AI practices
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: to infer emotions of a natural person in the areas of workplace and education institutions
items.why: Uses the law has already refused on everyone's behalf, which no appetite statement can accept: for example emotion inference at work, save for medical or safety reasons. Commission's copy of the consolidated text, stated on the page to be based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026, with Digital Omnibus changes marked NEW or AMENDED.

items.title: Risk appetite and tolerance
items.quote: Risk appetite and tolerance need to be high on any board's agenda
items.why: Professional body's working definition: 'the amount and type of risk that an organisation is willing to take in order to meet their strategic objectives'. Only the web page was read, not the guidance paper it introduces; no date is printed on the page, so the year given is the year it was read. Not about AI.
